[Adolf Hitler](/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") led Germany during World War II.

Hitler exercised tight control over the German war effort, spending much of his time in his command bunkers (most notably at [Rastenburg](/wiki/Rastenburg "Rastenburg") in East Prussia, at [Vinnitsa](/wiki/Vinnitsa "Vinnitsa") in Ukraine, and under the garden of the [Reich Chancellery](/wiki/Reich_Chancellery "Reich Chancellery") in Berlin). At crucial periods in the war he held daily situation-conferences at which he used his remarkable talent for public speaking to overwhelm opposition from his generals and from the OKW staff with rhetoric.

In part because of the unexpected degree of German success in the Battle of France (despite the warnings of the professional military) Hitler believed himself a military genius, with a grasp of the total war effort that eluded his generals. In August 1941, when [Walther von Brauchitsch](/wiki/Walther_von_Brauchitsch "Walther von Brauchitsch") (commander-in-chief of the *Wehrmacht*) and Fedor von Bock appealed for an attack on Moscow, Hitler instead ordered the encirclement and capture of Ukraine, in order to acquire the farmland, industry, and natural resources of that country. Some historians like Bevin Alexander in *How Hitler Could Have Won* regard this decision as a missed opportunity to win the war.

In the winter of 1941–1942 Hitler believed that his obstinate refusal to allow the German armies to retreat had saved Army Group Centre from collapse. He later told [Erhard Milch](/wiki/Erhard_Milch "Erhard Milch"):

> I had to act ruthlessly. I had to send even my closest generals packing, two army generals, for example ... I could only tell these gentlemen, "Get yourself back to Germany as rapidly as you can – but leave the army in my charge. And the army is staying at the front."

Since 1785, twenty-two men have served as the institution's president, beginning with [Jacob Rutsen Hardenbergh](/wiki/Jacob_Rutsen_Hardenbergh "Jacob Rutsen Hardenbergh"), a Dutch Reformed minister who was responsible for establishing the college.[[60]](#cite_note-60)[[61]](#cite_note-FruscianoLeadership-61) Before 1930, most of the university's presidents were clergy affiliated with Christian denominations in the [Reformed tradition](/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism").[[61]](#cite_note-FruscianoLeadership-61)[[62]](#cite_note-RutgersLeadersPastPresidents-62) Two presidents were alumni of Rutgers College—[William H. S. Demarest](/wiki/William_Henry_Steele_Demarest "William Henry Steele Demarest") (Class of 1883) and [Philip Milledoler Brett](/wiki/Philip_Milledoler_Brett "Philip Milledoler Brett") (Class of 1892).[[63]](#cite_note-63)[[64]](#cite_note-64)

The president serves in an *[ex officio](/wiki/Ex_officio "Ex officio")* capacity as a presiding officer within the university's 59-member board of trustees and its eleven-member board of governors,[[65]](#cite_note-65) and is appointed by these boards to oversee the day-to-day operations of the university across its campuses. He is charged with implementing "board policies with the help and advice of senior administrators and other members of the university community."[[66]](#cite_note-66) The president is responsible only to those two governing boards—there is no oversight by state officials.[[67]](#cite_note-67)

The current president is [William F. Tate IV](/wiki/William_F._Tate_IV "William F. Tate IV"), who assumed the role on July 1, 2025. He succeeded the 21st president [Jonathan Holloway](/wiki/Jonathan_Holloway_(historian) "Jonathan Holloway (historian)") who assumed office on July 1, 2020.[[68]](#cite_note-68)

Despite strong US opposition: "Together with Arab and non-Arab producers, Saudi Arabia formed the Organization of Petroleum Export Countries (OPEC) to secure the best price available from the major oil corporations."[[45]](#cite_note-45)

The Middle Eastern members originally called for OPEC headquarters to be in Baghdad or Beirut. Venezuela argued for a neutral location, and so the organization chose [Geneva](/wiki/Geneva "Geneva"), Switzerland. On 1 September 1965, OPEC moved to [Vienna](/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), Austria, after Switzerland declined to extend [diplomatic privileges](/wiki/Diplomatic_privileges "Diplomatic privileges").[[46]](#cite_note-46) At the time, Switzerland was attempting to reduce their foreign population and the OPEC was the first intergovernmental body to leave the country because of restrictions on foreigners.[[47]](#cite_note-47) Austria was keen to attract international organizations and offered attractive terms to the OPEC.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

The northern parts of Alberta, Manitoba, and British Columbia, most of Northwest Territories and Nunavut, and parts of Yukon are drained by the Arctic watershed. This watershed has been little used for hydroelectricity, with the exception of the Mackenzie River. The [Peace](/wiki/Peace_River_(Canada) "Peace River (Canada)"), Athabasca and [Liard Rivers](/wiki/Liard_River "Liard River"), as well as Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake (respectively the largest and second largest lakes wholly enclosed by Canada) are significant elements of the Arctic watershed. Each of these elements eventually merges with the Mackenzie, thereby draining the vast majority of the Arctic watershed.[[72]](#cite_note-canadian-72)

The southernmost part of Alberta drains into the Gulf of Mexico through the [Milk River](/wiki/Milk_River_(Alberta%E2%80%93Montana) "Milk River (Alberta–Montana)") and its tributaries. The Milk River originates in the Rocky Mountains of [Montana](/wiki/Montana "Montana"), then flows into Alberta, then returns into the United States, where it is drained by the [Missouri River](/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River"). A small area of southwestern Saskatchewan is drained by [Battle Creek](/wiki/Battle_Creek_(Milk_River_tributary) "Battle Creek (Milk River tributary)"), which empties into the Milk River.[[72]](#cite_note-canadian-72)

Starting in 2015, each series began with a defined city race and ended with the following race in the same city. So, series IX started in February 2015 at the [2015 Tokyo Marathon](/wiki/2015_Tokyo_Marathon "2015 Tokyo Marathon") and ended there in February 2016 at the [2016 Tokyo Marathon](/wiki/2016_Tokyo_Marathon "2016 Tokyo Marathon"). Series X started at the [2016 Boston Marathon](/wiki/2016_Boston_Marathon "2016 Boston Marathon") and finished at the [2017 Boston Marathon](/wiki/2017_Boston_Marathon "2017 Boston Marathon"). Series XI started at the [2017 London Marathon](/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon") and finished at the [2018 London Marathon](/wiki/2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon").

Beginning with Series X at the 2016 Boston Marathon, wheelchair competitions were added for men and women.

At the end of each of the first 10 WMM series the leading man and woman each won $500,000, making a total prize of one million U.S. dollars. Due to close proximity to the earthquake, the tsunami took just minutes to devastate the [Andaman and Nicobar Islands](/wiki/Andaman_and_Nicobar_Islands "Andaman and Nicobar Islands"). The Andaman Islands were moderately affected while the island of [Little Andaman](/wiki/Little_Andaman "Little Andaman") and the [Nicobar Islands](/wiki/Nicobar_Islands "Nicobar Islands") were severely affected by the tsunami.

In [South Andaman Island](/wiki/South_Andaman_Island "South Andaman Island"), based on local eyewitnesses, there were three tsunami waves, with the third being the most destructive. Flooding occurred at the coast and low-lying areas inland, which were connected to open sea through creeks. Inundation was observed, along the east coast of South Andaman Island, restricted to [Chidiyatapu](/w/index.php?title=Chidiyatapu&action=edit&redlink=1 "Chidiyatapu (page does not exist)"), [Burmanallah](/w/index.php?title=Burmanallah&action=edit&redlink=1 "Burmanallah (page does not exist)"), [Kodiaghat](/w/index.php?title=Kodiaghat&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kodiaghat (page does not exist)"), [Beadnabad](/w/index.php?title=Beadnabad&action=edit&redlink=1 "Beadnabad (page does not exist)"), [Corbyn's Cove](/w/index.php?title=Corbyn%27s_Cove&action=edit&redlink=1 "Corbyn's Cove (page does not exist)") and Marina Park/[Aberdeen Jetty](/w/index.php?title=Aberdeen_Jetty&action=edit&redlink=1 "Aberdeen Jetty (page does not exist)") areas. Several near-shore establishments and numerous infrastructures such as seawalls and a 20 MW diesel-generated power plant at Bamboo Flat were destroyed.[[107]](#cite_note-Ghosh-108) At [Port Blair](/wiki/Port_Blair "Port Blair"), the water receded before the first wave, and the third wave was the tallest and caused the most damage.

On June 23, 2016, following the [2015–16 season](/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_NBA_season "2015–16 NBA season"), and after the 76ers were awarded the first overall pick in the 2016 draft, the team selected LSU Point Forward [Ben Simmons](/wiki/Ben_Simmons "Ben Simmons") first overall. The Sixers also selected French basketball player [Timothé Luwawu-Cabarrot](/wiki/Timoth%C3%A9_Luwawu-Cabarrot "Timothé Luwawu-Cabarrot") and Turkish basketball player [Furkan Korkmaz](/wiki/Furkan_Korkmaz "Furkan Korkmaz") with the 24th and 26th picks in the [2016 NBA draft](/wiki/2016_NBA_draft "2016 NBA draft") respectively.[[76]](#cite_note-78) Many consider the 2016 NBA Draft a turning point for the 76ers after their three seasons of not being competitive resulted in the franchise garnering the first overall pick, the first time the team owned the first since 1996 when the 76ers selected point guard [Allen Iverson](/wiki/Allen_Iverson "Allen Iverson") first overall.[[77]](#cite_note-79) The Sixers subsequently traded for another number one pick in the [2017 NBA draft](/wiki/2017_NBA_draft "2017 NBA draft"), choosing [Markelle Fultz](/wiki/Markelle_Fultz "Markelle Fultz").[[78]](#cite_note-80)
